Whether you’ve been following the industry trends or you're a practitioner yourself, you’ve likely heard the news: WPP is reportedly looking to sell Burson. As WPP’s only dedicated PR powerhouse following the Burson Cohn & Wolfe (BCW) and Hill & Knowlton merger in mid-2024,  stands as one of the largest firm with over 6,000 employees and hundreds of global branches. However, word is that a the struggling British communications conglomerate has tapped Goldman Sachs for a strategic review that could lead to a future spin-off.


I stumbled onto this update right after dinner, still trying to wash away the lingering aftertaste of celery with a glass of water. The moment I read the headline—and I say this without exaggeration—my wig was gone, my wig has evacuated. Genuinely snatched. This hits home because Burson is where I started my very first full-time job right after I graduate, and processing this potential sale feels like a total mayhem.
# Yesterday Is History

I was accepted into Burson in Autumn 2024. After a prolonged interview process, it was such a breeze hearing the call from the human resources specialist and learning they had chosen me. Burson is a prestigious, respected brand in the agency world. The team is highly professionalized, representing the quality, depth, and dedication you would expect from a global agency. For industry practitioners, kickstarting a career at Burson is a high-profile starting point. At least, that is what I thought originally.

The team’s client was a top-tier Chinese smartphone manufacturer looking to expand into regions like India, Southeast Asia, and Europe. Consequently, most of the team’s work involved go-to-market communications, such as media outreach, influencer seeding, and developing communication strategies. I remember the very first task I was assigned was an influencer mapping evaluation. It was a spreadsheet featuring a list of planned influencers for seeding, including notable figures like Mrwhosetheboss. My job was to complete the additional information—subscribers, regions, and content orientation—coupled with a short profile addressing the key attributes, limitations, and risks of each influencer. As it was my first formal "assessment," I wanted to make sure it was fully baked. I finished the sheet at approximately 10 PM, and my leader was quite satisfied.

The other part of the job was, of course, monitoring—specifically retainer work rather than project-based tasks. In case you aren't aware, project-based work is a one-time purchase, while a retainer involves recurring tasks. Generally, the team produced two monthly reports covering brand news, daily and monthly share of voice, competitor analysis (Samsung, Apple, etc.), and more. To ensure you wouldn't panic when writing the monthly brief, I was required to browse the monitoring page on Meltwater daily and record news reports from designated media outlets in a spreadsheet. Additionally, I was told to use Brandwatch to record every single news item mentioning that manufacturer in specific regions—a "RAW data" database maintained entirely by manual labor.

And that was pretty much everything. I participated in two go-to-market projects, a few market entry insight reports, and countless hours of "news hunting." I left Burson in Spring 2025, predominantly because I did not fit the mode of the "ideal candidate" they were looking for—or rather, it was an inherent mismatch. To put it more straightforwardly, they were looking for an "android" employee: a dutiful student who does exactly what they are assigned. I should have seen the signs early on, as all the other account executives—the entry-level role in PR agencies—left within a fortnight of my arrival. But at the time, I figured "having a job is good enough in this economy," so I told myself to stick around until force majeure took over.

Navigating the resignation was difficult, but luckily, I managed to leave before being sent to an asylum. There were countless conflicts, negotiations, and emotional breakdowns during my time there, but I’ll keep those a secret for now. Later I received an interview invitation from Ruder Finn—another notable PR agency. Operating as a family business, it isn't as large as Burson, but also maintains a global network. The process was astonishingly fast; I was accepted within three days. Interestingly, my new leader added me on WeChat prior to my start date; according to the HR specialist, she was "quite enthusiastic and keen to have me on board".

Everything and everyone seemed peaceful at first. In the beginning, my main duty was drafting the "Monthly Intelligence Report" for an NGO client. It featured trends and frontiers in energy and sustainability, along with a fair amount of political content, where Trump was a frequent visitor. There were quite a few objections and disputes within the client’s team regarding the content, and the density of the reports was often greater than expected. Frequently, our only recourse was to ask them to delete the surplus.

But everything began to change in Summer. Shortly after we had a face-to-face meeting with the client at their Beijing office—located on Jianguomen Outer Avenue with cars rushing by underneath—they decided not to renew the annual framework. That was how we lost a client, or more accurately, a major source of income. Fortunately, we had another key client, a global social media giant, so the financial situation wasn't imminent. We handled two major offline events for them, which kept me quite busy during that period. My responsibilities included drafting and typesetting whitepapers, designing event visuals, creating slide decks, managing event vendors, and publishing promotional posts on WeChat subscription accounts. 

And that is how my leader became increasingly high-strung and stressed. We participated in a bid for a logistics company, but it flopped. I even sacrificed my weekend to work on the presentation deck and never applied for compensatory leave. Later, we joined biddings for a robotics company and a household-name tech giant; at the time, the outcomes for both remained unknown.

Besides, whether voluntarily or due to the circumstances, my leader began transferring tasks to me that were originally handled by other teams. Retrospectively, I view this move as her effort to mitigate the team's growing deficit. One of these tasks involved drafting a crisis-management report for the very same client I had worked for at Burson. Essentially, I had to organize and analyze several notable crisis-handling examples each month and produce insights—all for a marginal, hilarious ¥3,000 per month. Another task was managing the WeChat subscription account for an enterprise SaaS company, billed for a robbery price of over ¥5,000 per piece. Interestingly, the client was informed that the agency had a dedicated account executive, an experienced copywriter and a designer for the project; in reality, it was just me, if you don't count AI agents as labour force.

Eventually, I left Ruder Finn, and I guess you wouldn’t be surprised to learn even a fraction of what happened there. Fortunately, I remained emotionally stable, though I was still psychologcially "tortured"—to use the words of a former colleague, who is a very sweet lady. By now, the team I once worked for has come out of the woods; it seems I joined at the worst possible time, and now, that chapter had concluded.

# Today Is Not A Gift

As stated in the Buddhist scriptures, any outcome does not arise out of nowhere; rather, it is the result of many causes. I got my own imperfections, I was not very good at debriefing the client and mitigating their expectations, and requires some more polishing in project management. But that's for another time. I spent quite a lot of time after I left Ruder Finn trying to get everything reconnect, reorganised, and reconstructed by thinking about just one question: what future holds for the PR/Advertising industry. An industry that was once being consider a dominant force in shaping contemporary life, global promotional culture, and was a high-growth industry. And my answer is clear, this industry is pretty much in limbo. 

For more than a century, the industry and these agencies have branded themselves as conglomerates' companions in shaping influential and resilient brand images. References such as Roosevelt’s well-known quote, "be the president or else an advertising guy," added a layer of glory and prestige to the profession, illustrating how impactful the promotional industry could be in shaping public perception—not just for brands, but for politics and social awareness. As cited on Burson’s webpage: 

>We are here to reinvent how reputation creates competitive advantage - helping our clients lead, innovate and grow in today's complex operating environment.

These agencies once did something remarkable. When Steve Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, he worked closely with Lee Clow, an advertising executive at TBWA (currently a division of Omnicom). The two collaborated on some iconic campaigns, including the original "1984" spot. Later, they developed "Think Different," a campaign that reshaped Apple from a legacy company on the precipice of failure into a brand dedicated to game-changers and creatives, and its influence persists; variations of the slogan are still used occasionally, such as Tim Cook's open letter celebrating the company's half-century milestone.

This serves as a prime example of how companies collaborated with agencies in the past. At that time, the most common arrangement was the "Agency of Record" (AOR) model, in which a client granted an agency a central role in shaping marketing strategies, branding, business goals, and more. They often worked in close alignment: agencies were deeply integrated into corporate decision-making, and advertising or PR executives frequently served as a CEO’s personal consultant.

For example, in 1994, IBM consolidated its marketing by firing roughly 40 different agencies and moving to a single-agency model with Ogilvy. The goal was to leverage the "tremendous equity of the IBM brand name using a consistent and coordinated brand message" (Tilles, 1994). This decision initiated a strategic partnership that lasted for more than 30 years, producing iconic campaigns like "Solutions for a Small Planet" and "Think." Unfortunately, the two split in 2026 when Ogilvy declined to participate in IBM’s creative review. As reported, the decision was driven by "long-standing balance-of-trade issues between WPP and IBM rather than any concerns over Ogilvy's creative work" (Wong, 2026).

This situation highlights a primary problem: the peer-level relationship between agency and client has largely disappeared, representing a degradation from "companion" to "vendor."

## Complete Downgrade
In China at least, such "co-creation" level of narrative, imagery and strategy framing is absent. Agencies will make expansive, in-depth, polished slide decks for pitching, spending half an hour to explain the backgrounds, strategies, and competitor analysis. In reality, non of these ambitious slogans goes to the actual work once you secured an annual service framework. PR service is becoming increasingly commoditified, moving to a "grocery shop" or "production mill" model. These days, many key agencies engage in works that has marginal strategic involvements: like drafting posts for WeChat subscriptions, designing product factsheets, drafting press release, and pitching journalists.
